Rule: Each color-1 blob is an "anchor". Every non-background, non-1 connected component is a "stripe" attached to one side of an anchor; the stripe is tiled periodically (period = its minimal repeating unit at the anchor-adjacent end, else its full extent) away from its anchor to the grid edge, overwriting every cell in its rectangular path — this completes incomplete stripes, repairs cells that break the stripe's periodicity (e.g. test rows 23–24 near the left stripe), and lets a newly-extended stripe overwrite a crossing stripe (as in pair 1, where the vertical 4/2 line replaces the horizontal 2 with 4 at the intersection).

Verification against trainings: pair 1 — vertical stripe (4,2) above the lower plus extends up (odd rows 4, even rows 2) and overwrites (5,10)=2→4; horizontal stripe already reaches the edge. Pair 2 — horizontal stripe (4,2) above lower blob extends up to row 0; vertical (2,3) stripe already reaches the bottom. Test — left stripe [[4,3],[6,2]] extends down from blob A (fixes row 23 col3 6→4 and row 24 to [6,2]); stripe [[7,3],[2,5]] above blob B tiles up (even rows [7,3], odd rows [2,5], cols 9–10, rows 0–14); stripe [[2,4],[3,5]] below blob C tiles down (row 24 gets [2,4] at cols 14–15).

Rule: The largest connected object is the template; all other multi-cell objects are tiles at a common scale `s` (the gcd of their bounding-box dimensions). The output is the template scaled up by `s`, with each connected hole filled by the color of the tile whose `s`-downscaled shape matches that hole under rotation/reflection.

**Rule:** Every 3-cell arrow object (8-connected; 8 templates: four cardinal V-shapes and four diagonal 2×2-Ls) shoots a mark exactly 5 cells from its tip in its pointing direction. A mark on background paints 9; two marks landing on the same cell paint 1; a mark landing on an existing object recolors that entire object to 9. I chose this uniform arrow semantics over the 4-connected "diagonal-pair" heuristic because it explains every training cell via one mechanism and correctly recognizes the test's down-arrow {(2,8),(2,10),(3,9)} and left-arrow {(3,14),(4,13),(5,14)}, which the heuristic silently drops (leaving those objects' shapes unexplained).

Verification highlights: pair 1 — up-arrows land (9,1),(9,7),(9,14) and the down-left L also lands (9,7) → collision gives the 1; pair 2 — six up-arrows give the six 9s; pair 3 — eight up-left Ls give rows 1/9 marks, and the middle L lands on the second top L → whole object recolored 9. Test: E lands on object A → A becomes 9; G and H both land (9,14) → 1; single 9s at (0,9),(4,8),(8,4),(8,7),(8,9).

**Rule:** Each grid contains one or more rectangular frames drawn in color 0 (sometimes clipped by the grid edge, so only some corners exist). Objects that touch/cross a frame border are copied unchanged — one of them is always a *finished example* that shows the completion pattern. Every remaining object lies strictly inside a frame on a diagonal ray from a frame corner K and is "shot" toward the **nearest** corner on its diagonal: if it is ≥2 diagonal steps from K, its color fills the diagonal trail to K, K itself, and the 2×2 block diagonally outside K (pair 1, including the non-square clipped frame). If it is adjacent to K, the grid's demo decides the shape: when the demo covers K's cell (K filled — pair 3 and the test's 2-shape at (5,13)), paint K plus K's two outward side-neighbors; when the demo leaves K empty (pair 2's 6-cell ring around corner (9,11)), paint the 6-cell ring (both 2×2 squares adjacent to K, minus K).

I re-derived this from scratch: pair 1 gives the trail+corner+2×2 pattern for distance ≥2 (verified cell-by-cell on all four objects, including the 4×8 clipped frame shot at its TL corner); pair 2's demo ring has an empty corner → adjacent objects get the ring; pair 3's demo covers corner (6,6) → adjacent objects get corner+two outward arms (verified on all 5 frames). The test's demo (2-shape) covers corner (5,13) → the corner+arms variant applies to its five adjacent objects: 4→(2,2),(1,2),(2,1); 1→(7,7),(8,7),(7,8); 6→(5,20),(4,20),(5,21); 8→(12,20),(13,20),(12,21); 5→(14,6),(13,6),(14,7).

Rule: Extract every 4-connected component of non-background cells (background = most common color); sort components top-to-bottom by their topmost cell (tie-break: leftmost cell); output a single column in which each component's color is repeated once per cell in that component.

Verification reasoning: Pair 1 gives component sizes 1:5, 3:4, 2:5, 4:5, 6:3 in top-to-bottom order → 22 rows, matching. Pair 2 gives 8:7, 2:8, 3:9 → 24 rows, matching. The test input deliberately splits colors 1 and 3 into two disjoint components each, interleaved vertically (1, 3, 8, 4, 3, 1 by top row), so components — not colors — are the units; it yields 1×5, 3×3, 8×6, 4×6, 3×2, 1×3 = 25 rows.

```json

```

Rule: The existing 6-cells are water sources. Water falls straight down, recoloring 7s to 6; when water sits directly above a maximal horizontal run of ≥2 twos ("bar"), it spills across its own row from one cell left of the bar to one cell right of it (clamped to the grid), and every newly spilled cell continues falling. Isolated single 2s block falling but never trigger a spill (training pair 4 confirms this). Dimensions never change; 2s and original 6s are preserved.

I re-derived this from scratch and hand-simulated the exact algorithm below cell-by-cell on all 6 training pairs — every output matches exactly (including pair 4's single-2 blocking, pair 3's edge-clamped spills, and pair 5's bottom-row spills). I also hand-simulated the test input with this code: source columns 2 and 12; col 2 falls through the 1-wide gap between the two row-4 bars all the way to the bottom; col 12's water spills across row 3 over the cols-11–15 bar, streams down cols 10 and 13; the col-10 stream spills across row 5 over the cols-8–12 bar (col 7 end is blocked by the bar below), and the col-13 stream runs to the bottom.

Rule: Each input contains a 9×9 symmetric decorative pattern (a 3×3 arrangement of 3×3 blocks) with a background-colored (8) 3×3 hole at its center block. The hole is filled with block F built from the 16 cells ringing the hole: F's corners = the 4 diagonal-adjacent cells, F's edge-midpoints = the 4 cardinal-adjacent cells, F's center = the color of the 8 remaining side-adjacent cells (e.g. pattern cell (2,3)). Then the pattern's blocks are stamped one block-ring outward in a fixed template (verified identically in all 3 training pairs): one row above the pattern = rot180 of the top blocks at block-columns −1,1,3 (holes between); the pattern row itself at columns 0,1,2; the middle row extended left/right repeating [B12, B10, F, B12, B10]; one row below the pattern = bottom blocks at columns 0,1,2; and a final row = the top blocks unrotated in reversed order (B02,·,B01,·,B00) at columns −1,1,3 — all clipped to the original grid size, leaving background everywhere else. Output dimensions equal input dimensions.

Verification notes: every block position of the template was checked cell-by-cell against all three training outputs (e.g. pair 1 output rows 0–2 cols 0–2 = rot180(B00); pair 2 rows 13–15 cols 0–2 = B02; pair 3 rows 8–10 cols 15–17 = B12; pair 3 rows 14–16 cols 15–17 = B00), and the F rule reproduces the observed hole fills [[9,9,9],[9,6,9],[9,9,9]], [[7,7,7],[7,1,7],[7,7,7]], [[3,2,3],[2,5,2],[3,2,3]] exactly. For the test, F = [[4,1,4],[1,7,1],[4,1,4]] (center 7 read from pattern cell (2,3), consistent with the majority color).
